canonical_topic: Why natural gas breaks the storable-commodity forward-pricing model
definition: Natural gas doesn't fit the classic storable-commodity model where spot and forward markets are linked through buy-and-store arbitrage, because gas requires continuous new production and consumption, is difficult to store and transport, and has no intrinsic value apart from what it's converted into.
core_idea: Classic storable commodities (e.g., gold, stock certificates) link spot and forward markets because the asset is never "used up" and can be carried forward unaffected by short-term supply-demand shifts; natural gas fails this pattern, so long-term buy-and-hold investing doesn't really work in gas, and the spot/forward relationship that does exist is more complex and less reliable than in other markets.
key_points: In markets where spot and forward prices are linked, the commodity's quantity is roughly constant and it isn't consumed when used (e.g., a gold bar or a stock certificate), so it's unaffected by short-term supply/demand swings.
Natural gas requires a continuous supply of new production, has constantly shifting consumer demand, and is difficult to store and transport — breaking that classic linkage.
Gas has no intrinsic value by itself; only the products of burning it (heat, electricity) are valuable.
Gas held in storage is generally no easier to deliver than newly extracted gas, unless the storage facility happens to be near a consuming area.
The most common storage facilities are previously emptied gas wells.
Consequently, a long-term buy-and-hold gas strategy is essentially a bet on undeveloped gas reserves rather than a genuine investment strategy.
Traders instead use storage tactically to balance supply and demand over periods under a year (e.g., buying summer gas to sell the following winter).
The author notes a spot/forward relationship does still exist in natural gas forward prices, but it is more complicated and less reliable than in other (storable-commodity) markets.
relationships: Connects to the spot/forward volatility item and to forward price seasonality
trading_implications: Classic cash-and-carry arbitrage used in metals or financial assets doesn't transfer cleanly to natural gas.
Storage should be treated as a tactical, sub-annual balancing tool rather than a long-term investment vehicle.
caveats: Assuming natural gas forward pricing follows the same storage-cost/interest-rate-driven curve as storable commodities like gold.
Assuming stored gas is a viable long-term investment rather than effectively a bet on undeveloped reserves.
